name: Bad Times Dance
tagline: Uploads a single photo and returns a short AI-generated dance clip of that person.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Apps in this niche usually sell credit packs rather than seats.

verdictSummary: The product is a form, a job queue, and a progress spinner wrapped around an image-to-video model with a fixed dance motion reference. An agent can rebuild that shell in an afternoon, and if you are willing to pay a model host per clip you get essentially the same output. The gap is the model itself: doing this locally means a character animation pipeline on a serious GPU, plus the unglamorous work of making a stranger's face survive five seconds of hip movement without melting. Also unglamorous: the curated motion reference and the audio sync that makes the meme land, which is product taste, not code. Call it a weekend if you rent the model, longer if you insist on running your own weights.
coreLoopDIY: A local web page that takes a photo, sends it plus a stored dance motion reference to an image-to-video endpoint, polls the job, and hands back a five second MP4 with the track mixed in.
requirements: An API key for a hosted video model (fal, Replicate, or similar) or a 24GB+ GPU for open-weight character animation
A dance motion reference clip you actually have the right to use
Patience with queue times and reroll costs
whatYouLose: Someone else eating the GPU bill and the failed generations
A motion reference and music bed that were picked because they are funny, not because they were the first thing on disk
Face and identity consistency tuning that stops the output looking like a stranger wearing your head
Phone-friendly upload, share sheet, and a result you can post without re-encoding
Any guardrails around uploading photos of people who did not consent
moatNotes: The moat is rented, not owned: whoever runs it is also one API call away from the same model you are. The durable part is knowing which five seconds of motion is the joke.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the whole appeal is friction-free: you are on your phone, you are mildly amused, you upload one photo and get something postable in under a minute. Nobody in that mood is installing ffmpeg or provisioning a GPU. Paying a few dollars for a credit pack is correctly priced against the twenty minutes of setup plus per-clip inference you would pay anyway, and the hosted version has already burned through the reroll attempts to figure out which settings do not produce body horror.
notes: The app is a spinner with good taste in motion references. The code is the easy half.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user web tool called "dancegen" that turns one uploaded photo into a five second dance video.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, FastAPI, Jinja2 templates, vanilla JS. No React, no build step.
- SQLite via sqlite3 stdlib for a jobs table. No ORM.
- ffmpeg invoked via subprocess for trimming, audio mux, and final encode.
- Video generation via the fal.ai HTTP API using an image-to-video or character-animation model that accepts a driving motion reference. Read FAL_KEY from .env with python-dotenv. Do not hardcode secrets.

Flow:
1. GET / renders an upload form: one image file input, a dropdown of motion presets read from ./motions/*.mp4, and a submit button.
2. POST /jobs saves the image to ./uploads/, inserts a job row with status queued, and kicks off a background task.
3. The background task uploads the image and the chosen motion clip to the model endpoint, polls until done, downloads the result to ./outputs/, then runs ffmpeg to trim to exactly 5.0 seconds, scale to 720x1280, mux ./audio/track.mp3 if present, and write final.mp4.
4. GET /jobs/{id} returns JSON status. The result page polls it every 3 seconds and swaps in a video tag when status is done.
5. Failures store the provider error text and show it verbatim. No silent retries.

In scope: upload, preset selection, one job at a time, a /gallery page listing past outputs with delete buttons.
Out of scope: accounts, payments, telemetry, cloud storage, queues beyond a single in-process worker, mobile app, model training.

Ship ./motions/.gitkeep and ./audio/.gitkeep plus a README that states plainly: you must supply your own motion reference clips and audio, each generation costs real money, and the output quality is the model's fault, not the app's. Include a make run target and a .env.example.
